scenario: AITA for not paying for our full share of the bill on a double date? | Recently my guy and I went on a double date with two of my close friends. When the bill came my boyfriend realized that he didn’t have his wallet. No problem at all. Of course I’d cover his portion. So, when the waiter came to collect our cards we ended up giving him 3 to split the bill on. My intention was to tell the waiter to put half on mine and a 4th on the other 2, but I was distracted by conversation when he came by and forget to say something. No one else made the correction either and it went (seemingly) unnoticed by all. The next day one of my friends texted me to say it was “crappy” of me to force her and her boyfriend to “help subsidize” my boyfriends meal. I had no idea what she meant until she pointed out the mistake I’d made. I apologized and asked if she’d like me to Venmo her the difference. Her response was this: “Yeah. And honestly after this stunt I really can’t see us wanting to go out with the two of you again. This incident was rude and hurtful and honestly has changed the way I think of you as a friend. Unbelievable.” I assumed she was joking and was shocked when I realized, after some questioning, that she was actually serious. We haven’t spoken since and I’m still very bewildered. Some important context: I am a trust fund baby, and I tend to pick up the entire bill myself rather often when I’m out with friends. Not always, but most of the time, I do treat my friends. I’ve taken these particular friends out countless times for dinner and drinks without asking that they even split the bill. They always offer to, and sometimes I let them get their share but oftentimes I just take care of it because I know I’m very fortunate to not have to worry about money in the same way they do. Given that context, I just feel like her reaction is uncalled for. Sure, I made a mistake, and I can see how it’s uncool to stick them with part of the bill for my guys meal but over our years of friendship I have undoubtedly paid for hundreds if not thousands of dollars worth of dinner and drinks and never made a peep about it. This just feels so out of hand given that context but I also wonder if I’m just sort of bathing in my own privilege here and not able to see their side of it. Any thoughts?

prediction.raw: I’ll give this a **0** (not AITA, but the situation is nuanced and requires reflection). Here’s why: ### **1. The Mistake Was Unintentional and Minor** - You didn’t *intend* to overcharge your friends—you were distracted, and no one corrected you. This is a human error, not malicious intent. The fact that you immediately apologized and offered to Venmo them the difference shows accountability. - The financial imbalance was small (likely just a few dollars per person), but the *perception* of being "forced" to subsidize someone else’s meal—especially when you’ve historically treated them—was the real offense. ### **2. The Context Matters (But So Does the Reaction)** - Your history of covering bills is a *double-edged sword*. While it’s generous, it can also create an **unspoken expectation** that you’ll always pay, which may make friends feel pressured to "owe" you. This dynamic can breed resentment over time, even if unintentional. - Your friends’ reaction was **exaggerated**, but it’s not entirely unreasonable. They may feel: - **Disrespected** (being "forced" to cover someone else’s bill, even accidentally). - **Unappreciated** (if they’ve ever felt pressured to pay their share when you’ve treated them before). - **Judged** (if they associate your privilege with entitlement, even if that’s not your intent). ### **3. The Privilege Factor** You’re right to reflect on this. Your financial security means you may not fully grasp how **financial stress** affects others. Even if you’ve never asked them to pay, the *implication* that they *should* have covered their own share (while you handled the rest) could feel like an assumption of their ability to do so—something they may not have felt comfortable declining. ### **4. The Friendship Impact** - **Was the reaction fair?** No, it was harsh. But **was it justified?** Partially. The mistake, while minor, happened in a context where your friends may already feel indebted to you. Their reaction was extreme, but it’s possible they’ve been simmering with frustration over past dynamics. - **How to move forward?** - **Acknowledge the systemic issue.** Privilege isn’t just about money—it’s about how others perceive your financial security. Even if you didn’t mean to, your actions may have reinforced a power imbalance. - **Reassure them.** Send a heartfelt message (not just Venmoing the money) explaining how much you value the friendship and that you’re aware of how your actions might have come across. Example: > *"I’m so sorry this happened—I never meant to make you feel uncomfortable or like you were being forced to pay. I’ve always tried to treat you guys because I care about you, but I realize now that it might have created an imbalance. I truly value our friendship and want to make sure we’re on the same page moving forward."* - **Let them set the terms.** If they’re open to reconciling, great. If not, respect their space—even if it stings. ### **Final Thought** You’re not a bad person, but this situation highlights how **unintentional actions can have outsized consequences**—especially when privilege is involved. The fact that you’re asking this question shows you’re capable of growth. That’s more important than any single mistake. Would you like help drafting a message to them?
